unanchored_factual_samples: In the late 1980s, it was a subterranean service, a plumbing problem buried beneath the application layer, invisible to the CIO until it failed.
This narrative traces that arc—from the hardware-bound transaction wars of the 1980s to the relational jungle of the 1990s, and finally to the commoditization of the server itself.
When I arrived at Stratus in the early 1980s, the world of transaction processing was defined by a single, brutal metric: throughput per dollar, measured in DebitCredit transactions.
We were fighting a war of numbers against Tandem, and those numbers were the only language the market understood [tandem-tr-85-2-debitcredit-1985-ca207a].
The DebitCredit benchmark, born from an anonymous industry consortium paper in 1985, had finally given us a common currency [tandem-tr-85-2-debitcredit-1985-ca207a].

Before that, we spoke in Whetstones and MIPS, metrics that measured CPU speed but ignored the complexity of locking, logging, and network latency inherent in real-world transaction systems [tandem-tr-85-2-debitcredit-1985-ca207a].
At Stratus, I used the ET-1 and TP-1 frameworks to compare our fault-tolerant systems against Tandem’s [stratus-et1-tp1-tandem-dossier-1986-26871a].

I ghostwrote the Yankee Group study *The Future of Transaction Processing* in 1987, cementing the idea that transaction processing was a distinct category of computing, one that required specialized hardware and software [stratus-sales-support-competitive-news-1-2aac8d].
The cost-per-transaction on an IBM mainframe was a line item that could not be justified in the emerging client-server world.
I saw this clearly in the DEC corpus.
